Without a greeting, the letter opens with witnesses: "we" who heard, saw and felt, writing to "you." Then it tests what people claim. "If we say" (verses 6, 8, 10) returns as "the one who says" (2:4, 6, 9) and "If anyone says" (4:20).

The senses draw nearer: heard, seen, gazed at, felt. The letter builds on this. No one has gazed at God (4:12), yet "we ourselves have gazed and testify" (4:14); and spirits are tested by whether they confess Jesus Christ come "in the flesh" (4:2). "Fellowship," used in the letter only in this chapter, runs through the witnesses: "with us," then "with the Father" (verse 3). Read as "the word of life," verse 1 means a message; as "the Word of life," a person (John 1:1). The joy of verse 4 is the writers', made full as the readers join them; other copies make it the readers'. John 1:1-4. The Word was "with God," the life "with the Father": one Greek word for "with." There "the life was the light"; this chapter too passes from life to light. Deuteronomy 4:12. Israel heard but saw no form. The letter's first verse goes on to eyes and hands.

The word "message" returns once, at 3:11: "that we should love one another." The two messages meet in verse 7: after the claim of fellowship "with him" (verse 6), walking in the light brings fellowship "with one another." And those who walk there still need the blood that "cleanses." From verse 6 on, "you" drops away: the witnesses count themselves among those who sin. Each "If we say" goes deeper: we lie, we lead ourselves astray, we make him a liar. Psalms 51:2-4. David owns his sin "so that you are righteous when you speak." Confessing shows God "righteous" (verse 9); denying sin, "we make him a liar" (verse 10). John 3:20-21. Here too "does the truth" goes with the light: whoever does it comes to the light so his works "may be revealed," as sins are in confessing (verse 9).
